p: Chapter two. What They Actually Need.
Week two came in with snow. The plows had pushed it up against the old Centennial Lighting Works sign, and by Monday afternoon somebody had drawn a space station in it with a finger.

Tiago spent that Monday on his knees in the high bay with four rolls of blue tape. When he stood up there was a rectangle on the concrete eight meters long and four point four wide, HEARTH laid out flat, with a red X at one end for the hatch. Inside it he'd taped Wes's sketch from the first week: two crew quarters near the hatch, the galley in the middle, two more quarters past it, and the hygiene station at the far end. Smallest apartment in Colorado, he said. Four roommates. No balcony.

Helen Cho-Ramirez came on Wednesday. She was smaller than her voice on the phone, with reading glasses pushed up into gray hair and a carry-on she never set down. She didn't want coffee or a tour. She wanted the tape.
She stood on the red X for a long time. Then she walked the length of the module slowly, heel to toe, counting under her breath, and stopped in the square that was the galley.
Can I tell you why I'm going to be difficult about this? she said.

Give it a week. She looked down at the tape. Nine years ago I was the flight surgeon on console the night the old station's galley caught fire. A food warmer. Three in the morning their time. I had the crew loop in one ear and the cabin numbers in front of me, and for five minutes the only useful thing I could do was write down the time.
She took out her wallet and unfolded a yellow sticky note that had stopped being sticky a long time ago.
Sticky note, Helen's wallet. 0312 alarm. 0313 masks. 0315 commander: smoke in galley. 0317 all four at node. 0331 air clear

Nobody was hurt, she said. People say that like it's the end of the story. It was five minutes. One of them had earplugs in and his door shut, and he was the last one out, and I watched that clock the whole time he wasn't answering. She folded the note along its old crease and put it back. I've carried this around for nine years. I'd like it to be the only one.
Then she straightened up. Now show me where they sleep.
Rosie had asked Nadia the same thing about the purple rocket on the fridge. Nadia still didn't have an answer. She walked Helen down the tape.
Colleen's Flight Notes: ask the people who'll live in it.

On Saturday Colleen asked Nadia to meet her at Centennial Airport. Colleen was preflighting a borrowed single engine airplane in a wind that made Nadia's eyes water. Nadia told her about the tape, and Helen standing in the galley, and the sticky note.
Good, Colleen said, running her hand along the leading edge of the wing. Now you have a stakeholder. Most programs only have a customer.

The stakeholder needs and requirements definition process exists to find out what the people with a stake in the system need from it, in the environment where they'll use it, and to turn those needs into stakeholder requirements. Its inputs come mostly from mission analysis: the problem statement, the list of stakeholders, early life cycle concepts, early measures of success, and source documents like the contract. Then the work starts. You identify stakeholders, you elicit their needs, you build concepts of how the system will be used across its life, you turn needs into requirements, and you check those requirements with the people who gave them to you.

Elicit is the right word. People rarely hand you their needs. They tell you what they disliked about the last system, or what they think you asked. So you interview, you run workshops, you watch people work, you walk through scenarios, and you build mockups cheap enough to be wrong. Nobody ever told me what they needed from a display, Colleen said. They told me what they hated about the old one. You had to watch them fly.

How the exam asks it. Know the flow. Mission analysis hands this process a problem statement, stakeholders, and early concepts. This process hands system requirements definition a set of stakeholder requirements, and hands validation the criteria it will use.

Colleen climbed in and pulled a laminated card from the side pocket. Engine fire in flight. Somebody sat in a chair on a quiet afternoon and imagined my worst day, step by step, so I wouldn't have to invent it at three thousand feet.

That's what a scenario does. The handbook separates two kinds of concept. A concept of operations, or ConOps, is the organization's view: how Halo means to run its station and where HEARTH fits in its plans. It usually starts in mission analysis. An operational concept, or OpsCon, is the user's view of one system: how a crew will actually live, work, and respond in HEARTH. It's built here. Both are life cycle concepts, and so are the concepts for deploying, supporting, and retiring the system.

An OpsCon is made of scenarios. A day in the life covers the normal day. Off nominal and emergency scenarios cover the bad ones: fire, depressurization, a toxic leak, a sick crew member. Maintenance scenarios cover the person with a wrench. Each scenario names the actors, the steps, the conditions, and the timing. A good set of scenarios turns up needs that nobody would have said out loud.
How the exam asks it. ConOps is the organization's view. OpsCon is the user's view of a specific system. If a question asks how operators will use the system day to day, the answer is the OpsCon.

How do you know if this flight went well? Colleen asked, and answered it herself. There are three kinds of measure, and they stack. A measure of effectiveness, an MOE, says how well the system does its mission from the stakeholder's point of view, without naming a solution. An MOE here would be that all four crew reach safety within the time a scenario allows. MOEs show up in early form during mission analysis and get firmed up here.

A measure of performance, an MOP, describes how the system itself performs, in terms an engineer can measure: how long the hatch takes to open, how much air the cabin fans move. Good MOPs explain the MOEs. A technical performance measure, a TPM, is a critical performance number you track through development against a planned value and a limit, so you see trouble coming before the review. The MOE is whether we got there, she said. The MOP is how fast this thing cruises. The TPM is the fuel I check every leg, so I know before I'm out of options.
How the exam asks it. Stakeholder view and mission terms means MOE. A measurable system attribute means MOP. Tracked over time against a plan and a threshold means TPM.

A need is written in the stakeholder's words. Helen's is that if there's a fire while they sleep, all four get out or to a safe place before the smoke gets them. A stakeholder requirement turns that into a statement you can check: who, what, under what conditions, how well, with no design hiding inside it, traced back to the need and the scenario it came from.

This process produces the stakeholder needs and requirements, the OpsCon and other life cycle concepts, the MOEs, validation criteria, and the traceability that ties them together. System requirements definition uses the requirements next, to write what the system itself must do. Architecture uses the scenarios. Validation uses the criteria at the end of the V to show the system meets the need for real people in a real setting. Set that validation intent now, while it's cheap.

How the exam asks it. The system is validated against needs and stakeholder requirements, and verified against system requirements. Watch for answers that put a design inside a stakeholder requirement.

Systems thinking starts with a boundary. The system of interest is the thing you're responsible for, here HEARTH. Around it sit the systems it interacts with, such as the host station and the ground. Then there are the enabling systems that support it through its life, such as the test cell and launch services. Then there's the environment. Drawing the boundary is a decision. Drawing it too tight leaves out the things that make the system work or fail.

The crew belong in the picture too. In an emergency, the people are part of how the system behaves. No airplane has a landing distance, Colleen said, stepping down off the wing. The airplane, the runway, the wind, and me on a bad day have one. Egress time is like that. It belongs to the layout, the smoke, the hatch, and the crew together, and you only find it by looking at them together.
How the exam asks it. If every part passes its own check and the whole still fails, the answer is about interactions, the boundary, or emergent behavior.
Decision one. Walk it with me.
Helen had two days at FRO before her flight home. Amara had booked her into a conference room with a projector and a stack of Halo's old requirements documents.
Helen looked at the stack and then out the window at the high bay. I can read those on the plane, she said. What does Nadia do with the two days?
A. Have Helen and safety mark which of the old station's requirements apply to HEARTH.
B. Interview Helen in the conference room, one need at a time, from a prepared list.
C. Spend both days on the tape with Helen and safety, walking a day and a fire.
D. Send Helen and safety a questionnaire before she flies in, and go over the answers.

They walk it end to end, then again with the lights in the high bay turned down. Helen keeps stopping to say things she'd never have said in a conference room: the crew sleeps with their heads toward the hatch, they keep shoes clipped by the bunk, nobody can find a mask in the dark. Jun fills four pages.
That's the move. Elicitation draws needs out of people. Walking real scenarios in a mockup, with the stakeholder and the specialists together, brings out needs an interview list would never reach.

Thursday Amara caught Nadia at the coffee machine. Helen's great. I love Helen. But I've got a requirements review on the calendar and Halo's crew office is about to own two of your weeks. How long does this take, and what do I get at the end?
A. Trim the scenario work to fit the review date and finish it afterward.
B. Add a schedule line for stakeholder needs, weeks two to six, owned by Nadia.
C. Tell Amara that needs work on a crewed module can't be put on a clock.
D. Write a one page plan for the needs work and tie it to the review date.

It fits on one page. Elicitation sessions with dates, Halo's people named, the scenario set, the stakeholder requirements, and the validation criteria, all due the week before the review. Amara adds it to the SEMP and the schedule the same afternoon. Now Halo's two weeks are on my calendar too.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Project planning covers the technical work, not just the schedule. You named the activities, the people and resources, the outputs, and how you'll know you're done, and tied it all to the review it feeds.
Wes wanted the problem statement on one line at the top of every HEARTH document, and he had his own draft.
Deliver a ninety cubic meter habitat module for a crew of four, per the contract. Done. That's the problem.
A. Use Wes's line as he wrote it at the top of every HEARTH document.
B. Ask Helen to write the problem statement for Halo in her own words.
C. Write that Halo needs two egress hatches and a safe haven in the module.
D. Write the line around the crew and what they must live through.
Wes reads it. No volume in it. Nadia says the volume is a constraint, and it goes in the constraints list right under the sentence. He frowns at it and leaves it.

Exactly right. A problem statement describes the need and what success looks like, in the stakeholder's terms, without a solution. Constraints like volume are listed separately so they bound the answer without replacing the question.
Decision four. Where the box ends.

Jun had a context diagram up on the big screen. HEARTH was a box in the middle. Halo Station was a box off to one side with a power line drawn to it. There was no box for the crew and none for the ground.
The crew aren't hardware, he said. And ground control is Halo's. We don't build either one. Should they even be on here?
A. Add the crew and ground control as actors outside HEARTH's boundary.
B. Redraw the boundary around all of Halo Station and what it touches.
C. Keep the context diagram to the hardware FRO itself is building.
D. Add ground control as an actor and cover the crew in a human factors note.
Jun adds two boxes and eleven lines. The crew box ends up with more lines into HEARTH than the station does. Huh, he says, and doesn't say anything else for a while.
That's the move. Systems thinking starts with a deliberate boundary. HEARTH stays the thing FRO owns, and everything it depends on or affects goes in the context, so the analysis looks at the whole.
Decision five. A day in the life.
By Friday of week two Nadia had a folder of notes from Helen's two days, a stakeholder list that kept growing, and Helen's sticky note photographed on her phone.
Wes came by with Halo's old requirements in a binder clip. You've got plenty. Start writing shall statements. We'll figure out how the crew lives in it once there's something to live in.
A. Write the operations concept first, starting with a day in the life.
B. Ask Halo to write the operations concept for the module they'll operate.
C. Start the requirements from the notes and add an OpsCon later.
D. Adapt the old station's operations concept for HEARTH and a crew of four.
It takes a week. The day in the life alone turns up nine needs that weren't in anybody's notes, including where four people eat at once in a galley built for two.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. The operational concept describes how the system will be used, normal and off nominal, through scenarios. Writing it first means the requirements describe a system that works across a whole day, including its worst one.
Jun wanted to put the scenarios in the model. He'd sketched the fire scenario as a SysML activity diagram, with a lane each for the crew, HEARTH, the station and the ground.
Wes looked at it over his glasses. Halo's going to read a document. Write a document.
A. Write the OpsCon as a document and keep Jun's diagrams as a reference.
B. Write Halo's document now and let the model catch up after the SRR.
C. Model the scenarios with timing and generate the document from it.
D. Model each scenario down to the fans and valves the design will need.

Jun puts timing on every step and links each one to the need it serves. The document Halo reads comes out of the model. When Helen changes one step, the change shows up in both places, and the needs it touches light up.
Exactly right. Modeling the OpsCon makes the scenarios traceable, consistent, and analyzable. Timing on the steps means you can run them later instead of arguing about them.
Decision seven. Write it for the people.

The fire scenario was the hard one. Jun had numbered the quarters along the tape. One and two faced each other by the hatch. Three and four faced each other past the galley, the same walk on paper. Four's opening sat half behind the hygiene station's wall, the last bunk in the module. Tiago had started calling it the far quarter, and by Tuesday everyone did. Each quarter got a curtain instead of a door. It was one of the first things Helen asked for, and nobody argued.

Jun's first draft started with a galley fire and walked through the fire: detection, alarm, suppression. Helen read it on a video call from Halo and was quiet a moment. You've written it for the fire, she said. Write it for the people.
Odette had been on the call the whole time without a word. Put it in seconds, she said at the end. People hide in minutes.
A. Add the commander's steps, from alarm to hatch, with times.
B. Use the old station's fire procedure as HEARTH's scenario.
C. Keep the fire centered draft and add an evacuation step per procedure.
D. Rewrite the scenario from each of the four bunks, with times.

They write it four times, once from each quarter. One and two are short. Three and four both have to go through the galley. Four, the far quarter, starts behind a wall and ends at the back of the line, with the fire between the bunk and the hatch. Helen reads all four and says, There. That's the scenario.

That's the move. Emergency scenarios are about how people and the system respond together. Writing one from each crew position surfaces needs a single fire centered view hides: who's farthest, who passes the hazard, and how long each one takes.

Wednesday of week three Wes went down the scenario line by line in the high bay, defending his layout. Hatch opens in four seconds. The galley has an extinguisher. Every quarter meets its volume. Aisle's wider than the old station's. Show me the part that fails.
He was right. Every part passed. Nadia felt how much she wanted that to be the end of it.
A. Ask Odette for a hazard analysis of the galley as the fire source.
B. Walk quarter four's route to the hatch with Wes in the galley fire scenario.
C. Accept Wes's point that parts passing one at a time cover the scenario.
D. Move the galley to the far end of the module before anything else.

They stand in the far quarter. To reach the hatch, the crew member in it walks toward the galley, through the galley, and past it. Wes looks down the tape and doesn't answer right away. No single part did that, he says. The layout did.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Systems thinking looks at the whole: the parts, how they interact, and the environment. The far quarter problem comes from layout, smoke, and crew together. No part fails on its own, which is why reviewing parts can't find it.
Decision nine. How Halo keeps score.
Amara wanted measures for the requirements review. Halo's going to ask how we know HEARTH is a success. I'd like to say ninety cubic meters, delivered, on schedule. That's what's in the contract.
A. Report volume, delivery and schedule, the measures in the contract.
B. Report hatch opening time, air flow and alarm volume from the hardware.
C. Work out the mission measures with Helen, in terms Halo would use.
D. Report the pass rate on FRO's verification tests as the measure.

They settle on five with Helen. The first one reads like her sticky note: all four crew at a safe location within the time each emergency scenario allows. Amara reads it and stops. Halo will sign that.

Exactly right. MOEs say how well the system achieves the mission from the stakeholder's view, without naming a solution. They start in mission analysis and get sharpened with the stakeholders, and later they're what validation checks.
Decision ten. From her words to a shall.
Helen's need sat at the top of the needs list in her own words: if there's a fire at three in the morning, all four get out or to a safe place before the smoke gets them.
Nadia had to turn it into a stakeholder requirement by Friday. Jun had four drafts on the screen.
A. "The crew shall be safe in a fire," traced to Helen's need, with the details for later.
B. "From any bunk, each crew member shall reach a safe location within the scenario time."
C. Helen's own sentence about the three a.m. fire, kept word for word as the requirement.
D. "HEARTH shall have a second hatch at the far end, beside quarters three and four."

Jun links it to Helen's need, the four fire scenarios and the first MOE. The time stays marked as to be determined, with the rationale noted: the old station's five minutes is the starting point, not the answer.

That's the move. A stakeholder requirement turns the need into a checkable, solution independent statement with conditions and a measure, traced to where it came from. "To be determined" with a reason is honest. A design hidden in the requirement isn't.
Tiago found her at the edge of the tape on Monday of week four, still in his coat. So. Helen's going to ask how we prove it. What do we show her?
A. Leave validation to Halo after delivery, with its crew on its station.
B. Plan timed crew runs on the tape now and in the flight module later.
C. Time the scenarios in Jun's model, with walk speeds and smoke spread.
D. Show her that every requirement in the set has passed verification.

They write validation criteria for each emergency scenario: who runs it, in what conditions, and what counts as success, tied to the MOEs. The first runs can happen on the tape in a month. Tiago circles the last line. In the flight module. With crew. Lights out.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Validation shows the system meets the stakeholders' needs in its intended use. Building the criteria from the scenarios and MOEs now, and planning early and late runs, points the whole program at the right question.

They wanted a first timed walk on the tape before Jun built the depressurization scenario, to check the numbers in the model. Amara offered volunteers. I've got six engineers who'd love to leave their desks for an afternoon.
A. Use Halo's crew trainers who haven't seen the layout, starting in the bunks.
B. Have Helen walk it herself a few times and time each of her runs.
C. Use Amara's six engineers and time them on the tape this afternoon.
D. Use the old station's measured crew times in place of a walk on the tape.

Helen sends three trainers who've never seen the layout. Each one starts flat on a taped bunk, lights out, with an alarm on a speaker. The slowest one takes a wrong turn at the galley. Jun writes down every time to the second.

Exactly right. Validation evidence should come from representative users in conditions close to the intended use. People who don't know the layout, starting from where they'd really be, give numbers the model can trust.

Jun ran the depressurization scenario on Thursday night of week four, in the high bay, with his laptop on a folding table at the edge of the tape. Halo's reference leak. Alarm at zero. The target was all four through the hatch and the hatch closed by one hundred and twenty seconds. Jun had typed in the times from the tape, to the second.

HEARTH operational concept, scenario E2 (depressurization), model run 1. Reference leak. Alarm at 0 seconds. Hatch must be closed by 120 seconds.. Quarter 1: at hatch 53, through 68. Quarter 2: at hatch 53, through 83. Quarter 3: at hatch 67, through 98. Quarter 4: at hatch 67, through 113. Hatch closed at 133. Result: NOT MET, 13 seconds over. Last through: quarter 4.
Nobody said anything. Quarter four's bar, with the hatch time stacked on the end of it, ran past the red line on Jun's screen. It was a short way past, which somehow made it worse.
They'd come close to writing shall statements in week two. Not one of them would have had a number for the walk from quarter four. The scenario put one there.

Wes was the one who walked down the tape first. He stood in the far quarter with his hands in his pockets and looked at the red X eight meters away. Brooks, he said, not turning around. Good thing we didn't draw walls.

Nadia walked to quarter four and lay down on the cold concrete inside the tape, head toward the hatch, the way Helen said the crew slept. From the floor the red X looked a lot farther than eight meters.
She called Helen from there. It was late in Halo's time zone and Helen picked up anyway.
We timed it, Nadia said. Depressurization. A hundred and thirty three seconds. The scenario allows a hundred and twenty.
There was a pause on the line, long enough that Nadia could hear Helen breathing.
Three and four. Four's the last one out.
Okay, Helen said, and Nadia heard a wallet open on the other end. Now we know. Write it down exactly like you just said it to me.
